e-21597.knowledge_point: Identifying the System Given a Phase Portrait
e-21597.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/25d4f77a3f596202229581e06d88a9e3bdd84dc6b8b7e14b6f46b3b3d2f125d2.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

- ${\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t)\end{aligned}$

- ${\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=6y(t)\end{aligned}$

- ${\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-6y(t)\end{aligned}$

- ${\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-6y(t)\end{aligned}$
e-21597.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/343f6f32ac21a1bf06b86174734dd9ebba6ddb7598cbe83b4ade59f70e8e8b26.png)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/cb0f32e55af289452f1429ddfe3214a46501c55f3a61deaf10b4f736e47dca7f.png)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/85fdb4fc83a6f2b44178be2e97a0e7985d97350deb4e0fb123e513a80090906a.png)

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/3f984a493e976bd522455395defcb4c1562d61ca56e19fa27e2272832ce6011c.png)
must approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, we must have $\lambda_1 < 0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/44f82894493c95c38039bc1e6a842bb7226571e9818e3c10c50d33627464ea37.png)
must also approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, we must have $\lambda_2 < 0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies $\lambda_1 < 0$ and $\lambda_2 < 0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-5x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-6y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/470210fb9509e87c3e51a990bac7483e5862d2f37afdce9823279838e8391592.png)
e-21633.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/703fb7adc0ca076e42aecc781d4d0dc58eb5f4fec03db4d18bf5a36f7055a349.png)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/7210186106fc202e3b9a35ffa32b06b09493ce28c191a89c2824a35a547febff.png)

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_1=-1$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/f292220b15ff9b0d695cb8b9f2349cc275557fd2b77c32c147e25365ab0f7e47.png)

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_2=-4$ with the corresponding eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/5671487738e750f488ad61852f17fb4b6b14cf4050fee66338000d4939914ce6.png)

The general solution of the system is
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/651cc55c8b96c402fc00140c06736493e71276666ce4eb1ba74c2294600a1b89.png)

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/222dcd944fc89cd0f07970cddf5c50aa167c7f2d25b1f7305779c3dbb0a4a6af.png)
lie on the $x$-axis. Since $e^{-t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/08ad54b92f62513fb88f12f7bd6da358263e46673d686e0982a1e8044b8ab131.png)
lie on the $y$-axis. Since $e^{-4t} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ these solutions also approach the origin as $t \to \infty.$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/c5b1aa6ccde39c56b503e2d59a56e2ac8058b08495567f4e2cb40f6a056faedd.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t) = c_1e^{-t}$ and $y(t)=c_2e^{-4t}$ provided that $c_1,c_2 \neq 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{-4t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{-t})^{′}}=\frac{-4{c}_{2}{e}^{-4t}}{-{c}_{1}{e}^{-t}}=\frac{4{c}_{2}}{{c}_{1}}{e}^{-3t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\dfrac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} \to 0$ as $t \to \infty,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more horizontal as the trajectories approach the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/6c3af2fe68c4bcddbbfd9f13eb84e73014511374c0adc570084f9c92773d31e0.png)

e-21607.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=4y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Interpret the stability of the $x$-axis, the $y$-axis, and the equilibrium point (the origin) for the given decoupled system of linear differential equations.
e-21607.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/7f53fdda091242e4fee1edd70a7e96c649eff8bac93fcdc9fed6da38ec5c7523.png)
where ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/3b9909cba711a2394b8dbcda4b9d72ffbd9d37bd24b90506ac22b44c4cd398c4.png)

Recall that a homogeneous system of linear differential equations has a single equilibrium (fixed point) at the origin.

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_1=2$ with the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/1ea46da3e9697ee89d1112dfec53457657271c391a28a6c55267da70d38157c4.png) The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/9725d696549426d16093b7cd0e9bb188589472ed9ff81520c19a07ab296fb96d.png)
lie on the $x$-axis and move away from the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, the $x$-axis is the $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable}}$ line.

- Eigenvalue $\lambda_2=4$ with the eigenvector ![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/85e8d745e2b504770815bb92ad1a151f422c941874f33840593836e78eeaacde.png) The corresponding straight-line solutions of the form
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/2f67b02cda725daa0d0b994f3f4952065793e53ddc32260b14310f5158876f4f.png)
lie on the $y$-axis and also move away from the origin as $t \to \infty.$ So, the $y$-axis is the $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{unstable}}$ line.

Therefore, the equilibrium point (origin) is $\bbox[4pt, border: solid 1pt gainsboro]{\text{an unstable node (source)}}.$ 

**Note:** The phase portrait of the system looks as follows:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/2b79201d15fe5d2a9896cdee09c0474b97bb933d75fcf478c6fdb37cb4d16742.png)

decision.explanation: The solutions are x(t)=C₁e^{3t} and y(t)=C₂e^{-5t}. Thus trajectories move away from the origin along the x-axis and toward it along the y-axis. The origin is a saddle, with curved trajectories approaching the x-axis as time increases. Option e shows these directions.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & -5\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=-5$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{-5t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{-5t}\to 0$ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

\

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/3facfdf59a92a9202d834cd77d14e009c4ec69c5f1b7bd5f12bd17ea1bbc338b.png)

EXPLANATION

Writing our system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[300−5]x(t) where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

  • Eigenvalue λ1=3 with the corresponding eigenvector [10].

  • Eigenvalue λ2=−5 with the corresponding eigenvector [01].

The general solution of the system is x(t)=c1e3t[10]+c2e−5t[01].

Now, notice that:

  • The straight-line solutions of the form c1e3t[10] lie on the x-axis. Since e3t→∞ as t→∞, these solutions approach infinity as t→∞.

  • The straight-line solutions of the form c2e−5t[01] lie on the y-axis. Since e−5t→0 as t→∞, these solutions approach the origin as t→∞.

Among the given options, the only phase portrait satisfying these conditions is the following:

lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{4t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Writing our system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[−1004]x(t) where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

  • Eigenvalue λ1=−1 with the corresponding eigenvector [10].

  • Eigenvalue λ2=4 with the corresponding eigenvector [01].

The general solution of the system is x(t)=c1e−t[10]+c2e4t[01].

Now, notice that:

  • The straight-line solutions of the form c1e−t[10] lie on the x-axis. Since e−t→0 as t→∞, these solutions approach the origin as t→∞.

  • The straight-line solutions of the form c2e4t[01] lie on the y-axis. Since e4t→∞ as t→∞, these solutions approach infinity as t→∞.

Question 6
?

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=−7x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
b
{x′(t)=−3x(t)y′(t)=−7y(t)
c
{x′(t)=3x(t)y′(t)=7y(t)
d
{x′(t)=3x(t)y′(t)=−7y(t)
e
{x′(t)=−3x(t)y′(t)=7y(t)
Submit

decision.explanation: The arrows point away from the origin along both axes, so both eigenvalues must be positive. Option c has eigenvalues 3 and 7; its trajectories y=C|x|^{7/3} also match the displayed outward-curving portrait.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/f69ae5c2aeaa84d0e1b9b58da90ec738bf47a8f3c69145b990e12f13e25503e7.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
after.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}>0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=−7x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
b
{x′(t)=−3x(t)y′(t)=−7y(t)
c
{x′(t)=3x(t)y′(t)=7y(t)
d
{x′(t)=3x(t)y′(t)=−7y(t)
e
{x′(t)=−3x(t)y′(t)=7y(t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[λ100λ2]x(t) where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10]andc2eλ2t[01].

Now, notice that:

  • The tangents along the x-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ1>0.

  • The tangents along the y-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[01] must also approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ2>0.

Among the options, the only system that satisfies λ1>0 and λ2>0 is the following: {x′(t)=3x(t)y′(t)=7y(t)

content.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}>0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=−4x(t)y′(t)=−y(t)
b
{x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=y(t)
c
{x′(t)=−4x(t)y′(t)=y(t)
d
{x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=−y(t)
e
{x′(t)=−y(t)y′(t)=−4y(t)
Submit

decision.explanation: The arrows point away from the origin along the x-axis and toward it along the y-axis. Thus the x coefficient is positive and the y coefficient is negative. Option d satisfies these conditions, with trajectories y=C|x|^{-1/4} matching the displayed saddle portrait.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/aaeba63f6237121fe226eb30e5378d3e93129bb2782b9c8acb8d73ac719676b3.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
after.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=−4x(t)y′(t)=−y(t)
b
{x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=y(t)
c
{x′(t)=−4x(t)y′(t)=y(t)
d
{x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=−y(t)
e
{x′(t)=−y(t)y′(t)=−4y(t)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[λ100λ2]x(t) where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10]andc2eλ2t[01].

Now, notice that:

  • The tangents along the x-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ1>0.

  • The tangents along the y-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[01] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ2<0.

Among the options, the only system that satisfies λ1>0 and λ2<0 is the following: {x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=−y(t)

verification.explanation: The portrait has outward arrows along the x-axis and inward arrows along the y-axis, requiring a positive x coefficient and a negative y coefficient. Option d satisfies this and agrees with the revealed solution. The incorrect feedback refers to the deliberately submitted option c.

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/aaeba63f6237121fe226eb30e5378d3e93129bb2782b9c8acb8d73ac719676b3.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
content.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10]andc2eλ2t[01].

  • The tangents along the y-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[01] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ2<0.

Among the options, the only system that satisfies λ1>0 and λ2<0 is the following: {x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=−y(t)

Your Answer:
{x′(t)=−4x(t)y′(t)=y(t)

Question 8
?

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=5x(t)y′(t)=−2y(t)
b
{x′(t)=−2x(t)y′(t)=−5y(t)
c
{x′(t)=2x(t)y′(t)=5y(t)
d
{x′(t)=−2x(t)y′(t)=5y(t)
e
{x′(t)=2x(t)y′(t)=−5y(t)
Submit

decision.explanation: Arrows along both axes point toward the origin, so both coefficients must be negative. Option b has solutions x(t)=C₁e^{-2t} and y(t)=C₂e^{-5t}, with trajectories y=C|x|^{5/2} matching the displayed stable node.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/039bae0d2eedf7d12d8283b2b134855c531efcba1bd0fa14fe9f841b28d5204e.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
after.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=5x(t)y′(t)=−2y(t)
b
{x′(t)=−2x(t)y′(t)=−5y(t)
c
{x′(t)=2x(t)y′(t)=5y(t)
d
{x′(t)=−2x(t)y′(t)=5y(t)
e
{x′(t)=2x(t)y′(t)=−5y(t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[λ100λ2]x(t) where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10]andc2eλ2t[01].

Now, notice that:

  • The tangents along the x-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ1<0.

  • The tangents along the y-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[01] must also approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ2<0.

Among the options, the only system that satisfies λ1<0 and λ2<0 is the following: {x′(t)=−2x(t)y′(t)=−5y(t)

content.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-2x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-5y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=−6x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
b
{x′(t)=3x(t)y′(t)=−6y(t)
c
{x′(t)=6x(t)y′(t)=3y(t)
d
{x′(t)=6x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
e
{x′(t)=−6x(t)y′(t)=3y(t)
Submit

decision.explanation: The arrows point toward the origin along both axes, requiring both coefficients to be negative. Option a gives x(t)=C₁e^{-6t} and y(t)=C₂e^{-3t}; its trajectories y=C|x|^{1/2} approach the origin tangent to the y-axis, matching the portrait.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/a6a2a93d3fdf38eb57b5183a8d8c5d87f8524f976b5c8827e4717c0aeaf69200.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
after.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-6x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=−6x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
b
{x′(t)=3x(t)y′(t)=−6y(t)
c
{x′(t)=6x(t)y′(t)=3y(t)
d
{x′(t)=6x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
e
{x′(t)=−6x(t)y′(t)=3y(t)
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[λ100λ2]x(t) where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10]andc2eλ2t[01].

Now, notice that:

  • The tangents along the x-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10] must approach the origin as t→∞. So, we must have λ1<0.

content.problem:

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
content.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}<0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing toward the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach the origin as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}<0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}<0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}<0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=-6x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=3y(t)
b
{x′(t)=−4x(t)y′(t)=3y(t)
c
{x′(t)=−3x(t)y′(t)=−4y(t)
d
{x′(t)=−4x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
e
{x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
Submit

decision.explanation: The arrows point away from the origin along both axes, so both coefficients must be positive. Option a gives x(t)=C₁e^{4t} and y(t)=C₂e^{3t}, with trajectories y=C|x|^{3/4} matching the outward-curving portrait.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/5243b22ebef45709f214ac2422cfb72528f24fd5ef51bd38aa3fc0ff40f1888d.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
after.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}>0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above. Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?

a
{x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=3y(t)
b
{x′(t)=−4x(t)y′(t)=3y(t)
c
{x′(t)=−3x(t)y′(t)=−4y(t)
d
{x′(t)=−4x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
e
{x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=−3y(t)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have x′(t)=[λ100λ2]x(t) where x(t)=[x(t)y(t)].

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10]andc2eλ2t[01].

Now, notice that:

  • The tangents along the x-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c1eλ1t[10] must approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ1>0.

  • The tangents along the y-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form c2eλ2t[01] must also approach infinity as t→∞. So, we must have λ2>0.

Among the options, the only system that satisfies λ1>0 and λ2>0 is the following: {x′(t)=4x(t)y′(t)=3y(t)

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/5243b22ebef45709f214ac2422cfb72528f24fd5ef51bd38aa3fc0ff40f1888d.png)

Consider the phase portrait for a decoupled system above.
Which of the following systems could correspond to the given portrait?
content.worked_solution:
Writing a decoupled system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}{\lambda }_{1} & 0 \\ 0 & {\lambda }_{2}\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are parallel to the axes. These correspond to so-called straight-line solutions of the form

$$
{c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\,\text{and}\,{c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The tangents along the $x$-axis are pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{1}{e}^{{\lambda }_{1}t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
must approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{1}>0.$

- The tangents along the $y$-axis are also pointing away from the origin, meaning that the solutions of the form 
${c}_{2}{e}^{{\lambda }_{2}t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
must also approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$ So, we must have ${\lambda }_{2}>0.$

Among the options, the only system that satisfies ${\lambda }_{1}>0$ and ${\lambda }_{2}>0$ is the following:

$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=4x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=3y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: Both eigenvalues are positive, so arrows point away from the origin along both axes. Eliminating t from x=C₁e^{3t} and y=C₂e^{7t} gives y=C|x|^{7/3}, whose tangent is horizontal near the origin and becomes steeper outward. Option e matches both the directions and curvature.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
$$
{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=3x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=7y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Which of the following could represent the phase portrait of the decoupled system above?
after.worked_solution:
Writing our system in matrix form, we have

$$
{x}^{′}(t)=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 0 & 7\end{aligned}]x(t)
$$

where $x(t)=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}].$

Since our system is decoupled, its eigenvectors are the following:

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{1}=3$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}].$

- Eigenvalue ${\lambda }_{2}=7$ with the corresponding eigenvector $[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

The general solution of the system is

$$
x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]+{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, notice that:

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{1}{e}^{3t}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $x$-axis. Since ${e}^{3t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

- The straight-line solutions of the form
${c}_{2}{e}^{7t}[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$
lie on the $y$-axis. Since ${e}^{7t}\to \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ these solutions approach infinity as $t\to \infty .$

Among the given options, there are two phase portraits satisfying these conditions:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/96801605aa5d777eb18c13ded1f7b7e59ae74968b210da3b7a26f339a1c9f673.png)

Let's consider the solutions $x(t)={c}_{1}{e}^{3t}$ and $y(t)={c}_{2}{e}^{7t}$ provided that ${c}_{1},{c}_{2}\ne 0.$ Then,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{{y}^{′}(t)}{{x}^{′}(t)}=\frac{({c}_{2}{e}^{7t})^{′}}{({c}_{1}{e}^{3t})^{′}}=\frac{7{c}_{2}{e}^{7t}}{3{c}_{1}{e}^{3t}}=\frac{7{c}_{2}}{3{c}_{1}}{e}^{4t}.\end{aligned}
$$

So, $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\to \pm \infty $ as $t\to \infty ,$ meaning that the tangents to the solution become more and more vertical as we move away from the origin. This corresponds to the following phase portrait:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/differential/14069185/assets/20ef7519d0ca517d0d7d06d2998f7bd6c77f04145243f721e197fbef5c087791.png)
